tutorial_grammar.title: Verb Tenses in Interviews
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: When to use each tense
tutorial_grammar.content: Choosing the right verb tense tells the interviewer WHERE in time your experience happened. Using the wrong tense creates confusion and makes you sound unprepared.

sections.heading: Simple Past
sections.text: Use for completed actions at a previous job.
examples: I led a team of five engineers.
I reduced deployment time by 40%.
I built the authentication system from scratch.
sections.tip: If the job is over → Simple Past.

sections.heading: Simple Present
sections.text: Use for your current role and general truths.
examples: I manage three ongoing projects.
I work closely with the design team.
I specialize in backend development.

sections.heading: Present Perfect
sections.text: Use when experience started in the past but is still relevant now.
examples: I have worked with cloud systems for 4 years.
I have led multiple successful product launches.
I have always been passionate about clean code.
sections.tip: Experience that spans until now → Present Perfect.

tutorial_grammar.title: Formal vs. Informal Language
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: Sound professional, not casual
tutorial_grammar.content: Interviews are formal contexts. Using casual language signals a lack of professionalism. Small word choices make a big difference in how you are perceived.

sections.heading: Word Choices
sections.text: Replace casual words with professional equivalents.
examples: ❌ I did some stuff with Python → ✅ I developed data pipelines using Python.
❌ My boss told me to fix it → ✅ My manager requested a solution.
❌ It was pretty good → ✅ The outcome was highly effective.
❌ I worked on a lot of things → ✅ I managed multiple concurrent responsibilities.
sections.tip: Avoid: stuff, things, a lot, pretty, basically, kind of.

sections.heading: Contractions
sections.text: In formal speech, avoiding contractions sounds more polished.
examples: ❌ I don't have experience with X, but I'm a fast learner.
✅ I do not have direct experience with X, but I am a quick learner.
sections.tip: In interviews, natural speech with some contractions is fine — the key is avoiding slang.

sections.heading: Filler Words
sections.text: Filler words make you sound uncertain and unprepared.
examples: ❌ So, um... I was like, basically working on this thing...
✅ [pause] In my previous role, I was responsible for...
sections.tip: A confident pause is better than 'um', 'uh', 'like', or 'you know'.

tutorial_grammar.title: Quantifying Achievements
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: Turn vague answers into powerful ones
tutorial_grammar.content: Numbers make your answers concrete and credible. An answer with data is always more persuasive than one without. This is one of the highest-impact skills for English interviews.

sections.heading: The Formula
sections.text: Action Verb + What You Did + Result with a Number
examples: Reduced API response time by 65% through query optimization.
Increased team sprint velocity by 20% by introducing async standups.
Delivered the project 3 weeks ahead of schedule, saving $40,000.
Onboarded and mentored 4 junior developers within 6 months.
sections.tip: Can't remember exact numbers? Use approximations: 'approximately', 'roughly', 'around 30%'.

sections.heading: Strong Action Verbs
sections.text: Start your achievements with powerful verbs — not weak ones.
examples: ❌ Helped with → ✅ Led / Spearheaded / Orchestrated
❌ Worked on → ✅ Developed / Built / Implemented / Engineered
❌ Was responsible for → ✅ Managed / Owned / Oversaw / Directed
❌ Did some improvements → ✅ Optimized / Streamlined / Refactored / Reduced
sections.tip: Your resume and interview answers should start sentences with strong past-tense verbs.

tutorial_grammar.title: The STAR Method
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: How to structure behavioral answers
tutorial_grammar.content: STAR is the most effective structure for answering behavioral interview questions ('Tell me about a time when...'). It turns rambling answers into clear, compelling stories.

sections.heading: S — Situation
sections.text: Set the scene. Give just enough context — don't over-explain.
examples: "We were three weeks from the product launch and our lead backend developer unexpectedly resigned."

sections.heading: T — Task
sections.text: Define YOUR specific responsibility in that situation.
examples: "As the senior developer, I was responsible for either covering the missing work or quickly onboarding a replacement."
sections.tip: Use 'I', not 'we'. The interviewer wants to know YOUR role.

sections.heading: A — Action
sections.text: Describe exactly what YOU did. This is the most important part.
examples: "I immediately audited the outstanding tasks, reprioritized the backlog with the PM, took on the core API work myself, and requested a contractor to cover the remaining frontend tasks."
sections.tip: The more specific the action, the more credible and impressive the answer.

sections.heading: R — Result
sections.text: Quantify the outcome. What changed because of your actions?
examples: "We launched on time, with all core features complete. The product achieved 500 signups in the first week."
sections.tip: If you don't have a number, describe the qualitative impact: 'the team's morale improved significantly'.

tutorial_grammar.title: Professional Phrases Toolkit
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: Ready-made phrases for any interview moment
tutorial_grammar.content: Having a set of professional phrases ready helps you buy time, sound confident, and pivot gracefully in any interview situation.

sections.heading: Buying Time
sections.text: Use these when you need a moment to think.
examples: "That's a great question — let me think for a moment."
"Could I take a second to organize my thoughts?"
"I want to make sure I give you a complete answer..."
sections.tip: A thoughtful pause sounds far better than a rushed, incoherent answer.

sections.heading: Asking for Clarification
sections.text: Use these when you are unsure about the question.
examples: "Could you elaborate a bit more on what you mean by...?"
"Just to make sure I understand — are you asking about X or Y?"
"Would it be helpful if I focused on a specific example?"
sections.tip: Asking for clarification is a sign of intelligence, not confusion.

sections.heading: Transitioning Between Points
examples: "Building on that point..."
"Another relevant example would be..."
"To put that in context..."
"What's particularly relevant here is..."
sections.tip: Avoid: 'And also', 'Like I said', 'So yeah'. Use connectors that flow naturally.

sections.heading: Closing Strong
sections.text: Phrases to wrap up your answer confidently.
examples: "Ultimately, the outcome demonstrated that..."
"Looking back, the key lesson was..."
"That experience reinforced my belief that..."
sections.tip: A strong closing signals self-awareness and reflection — qualities interviewers love.

tutorial_grammar.title: Pronunciation & Clarity
tutorial_grammar.subtitle: Being understood is as important as what you say
tutorial_grammar.content: In a professional English interview, clarity of speech matters enormously. Even with accent, a clear, paced, and confident delivery is respected worldwide.

sections.heading: Pace
sections.text: Most non-native speakers speak too fast when nervous. Slow down.
examples: Pause between sentences — it gives weight to your words.
Breathe. A calm breath before answering signals confidence.
Rushing makes you seem nervous; pausing makes you seem thoughtful.
sections.tip: Record yourself answering a practice question. Play it back. Are you rushing?

sections.heading: Key Technical Terms
sections.text: Pronounce technical terms correctly — interviewers notice.
examples: Agile → /ˈædʒ.aɪl/ (not 'ah-JILE')
Cache → /kæʃ/ (like 'cash')
Queue → /kjuː/ (like 'cue')
Schema → /ˈskiː.mə/ (SKEE-ma)
SQL → 'ess-queue-ell' or 'sequel' (both are acceptable)
sections.tip: When in doubt, listen to native speakers say the term on YouTube.

sections.heading: Confidence Signals
sections.text: Non-verbal cues in a video or in-person interview.
examples: Eye contact — look at the camera (not your own image) in video calls.
Posture — sit upright; it actually improves how you sound.
Smile at the beginning — it immediately sets a positive tone.
Nod while the interviewer speaks — shows active engagement.
sections.tip: Your body language communicates as much as your words.
